# Shipworm and copper sheathing (`copper_sheathing_shipworm`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: needs copper_bronze; helped by ship_design_caravel_carrack, electrolysis
- Core idea: In warm seas the shipworm (Teredo, a boring clam, not a worm) riddles oak planks in months, and weed and barnacles slow a ship by a third. Nail thin copper sheets over the underwater hull: copper is poisonous to the larvae and to fouling, so ships stay fast and sound for years. Fasten the copper with copper or bronze bolts, never iron, because iron touching copper in seawater corrodes away (galvanic action). Cheaper stopgaps: an extra layer of sacrificial planking over tar and hair, charring, and regular careening and burning off the growth.
- Pitfalls:
  - Iron bolts under copper sheathing; they dissolve and ships founder (the Royal Navy's lesson of the 1770s–80s)
  - Lead sheathing as a cure-all; it is heavy, soft and also eats iron fastenings
  - Calling the shipworm a worm and expecting it in cold northern waters only; it thrives in warm water (Columbus's fourth-voyage ships were eaten through and beached in Jamaica, 1503)
- History: rome: 1st c. AD – lead sheathing on the Nemi ships and some merchantmen; china: Song–Ming – hulls coated with a lime, tung oil and hemp putty; europe: 16th c. – Spanish ships lead-sheathed; 1761 HMS Alarm trial with copper; by 1781 most of the Royal Navy coppered, copper-alloy bolts patented 1783–84; 1824 Davy's zinc protectors (cathodic protection)
- Read:
  - J. R. Harris, Copper and Shipping in the Eighteenth Century, Economic History Review 19 (1966)
  - Lincoln P. Paine, The Sea and Civilization: A Maritime History of the World (2013)
